questions.question: For a 4-hour battery at ERCOT's hub average with perfect foresight, what was the total revenue over the last twelve complete months (2025-10 to 2026-09), in USD per kW?
questions.answer: A 4-hour battery at ERCOT's hub average (ercot:HB_HUBAVG) with perfect foresight earned a total of 81.40 USD/kW of rated power over the 12 local months 2025-10 to 2026-09 (battery_stack_monthly, derived). That is the sum of 12 monthly total revenues (foresight_4h_revenue_total, energy plus ancillary). The same sum is 81,402.19 USD/MW. The monthly values ran from 3.60 USD/kW in 2026-06 to 14.63 USD/kW in 2026-01. All 365 days in those months were held and none were left out. Perfect foresight is an upper bound. The model assumes the battery is a price taker, reserves are paid and never called, and no capacity payment is included.

questions.question: What did a 4-hour battery with perfect foresight at ERCOT's hub average earn in total in calendar year 2021, the year of Winter Storm Uri, in USD per kW?
questions.answer: A 4-hour battery with perfect foresight at ERCOT's HB_HUBAVG earned 3,430.56 USD/kW in total (energy plus ancillary services) in calendar year 2021 (battery_stack_monthly, derived). This is the sum of the 12 monthly foresight_4h_revenue_total values, using local months from January to December 2021. No days were left out in any month. Winter Storm Uri in February 2021 drives much of this figure. Perfect foresight is an upper bound, and the battery is modelled as a price taker with no capacity payment.

# ISO-NE: the written layer

## What this grid is and who runs it

ISO New England (ISO-NE) runs the power grid and the wholesale electricity market for the six New England states: Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont. It is a nonprofit grid operator that owns no power plants: it schedules the plants that others own, keeps supply equal to demand, and plans the transmission system. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) approves its market rules.

Sources: https://www.iso-ne.com/about ; https://www.iso-ne.com/about/key-stats ; https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php

## How its market sets prices

ISO-NE runs a day-ahead market, where power for each hour of tomorrow is bought and sold today, and a real-time market, where plants are dispatched every few minutes. Prices are set at each location and reported for its load zones and one reference price, the Internal Hub, which this page uses. ISO-NE also runs a capacity market, the Forward Capacity Market, that pays resources to be available in a future year.

Sources: https://www.iso-ne.com/about/key-stats ; https://www.iso-ne.com/markets-operations/markets/forward-capacity-market ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/wholesale/

## What makes it different

Winter gas. New England makes much of its electricity from natural gas, but it sits at the end of the pipelines, and in cold snaps homes use that same gas for heat. When the pipelines are full, gas and power prices can jump, and the grid leans on oil, imported liquefied natural gas and power from neighbors. Winter, not summer, is often the season to watch here.

Sources: https://www.iso-ne.com/about/key-stats ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/dashboard/electric_overview/balancing_authority/ISNE

## A short history

- **1997:** ISO New England is created to run the region's grid independently of the utilities (ISO-NE, https://www.iso-ne.com/about/who-we-are/our-history).
- **2003:** ISO-NE starts pricing power by location, with day-ahead and real-time markets (Standard Market Design) (ISO-NE, https://www.iso-ne.com/about/who-we-are/our-history).
- **2008-02:** ISO-NE holds its first Forward Capacity Auction (ISO-NE, https://www.iso-ne.com/about/who-we-are/our-history).

Sources: https://www.iso-ne.com/about ; https://www.iso-ne.com/markets-operations/markets/forward-capacity-market

## Glossary

- **Balancing authority:** the organization that keeps supply and demand equal in an area. EIA reports ISO-NE as balancing authority ISNE.
- **Demand:** how much electricity customers are using, in megawatts (MW).
- **Megawatt (MW) and megawatt-hour (MWh):** a megawatt is a rate of power; a megawatt-hour is one megawatt for one hour, an amount of energy.
- **Net generation:** the power plants produce, minus what they use themselves.
- **Day-ahead market:** trades for each hour of tomorrow, agreed today.
- **Real-time market:** the price paid for power at the moment it is delivered.
- **Internal Hub:** ISO-NE's reference price, an average of locations in the middle of the region.
- **Forward Capacity Market:** ISO-NE's market that pays resources to be available in a future year.
- **Liquefied natural gas (LNG):** natural gas cooled into a liquid so it can travel by ship.
- **Carbon intensity:** the carbon dioxide released per megawatt-hour of electricity, in kilograms of CO2 per MWh.

Sources: https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/about ; https://www.iso-ne.com/about/key-stats

out.text:
# MISO: the written layer

## What this grid is and who runs it

The Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) runs the power grid and wholesale market across much of the middle of the country, from Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan south through Iowa, Illinois, Indiana and Missouri to Arkansas, Mississippi, Louisiana and East Texas, and into the Canadian province of Manitoba (MISO, https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/). It owns no power plants: it schedules the plants that its members own, keeps supply equal to demand, and plans transmission. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) approves its market rules.

Sources: https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/ ; https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php

## How its market sets prices

MISO runs a day-ahead market, where power for each hour of tomorrow is bought and sold today, and a real-time market, where plants are dispatched every few minutes. Prices are set at each location (locational marginal prices) and summarized at trading hubs; this page uses the Indiana Hub. MISO also holds a yearly capacity auction for the coming planning year.

Sources: https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/ ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/wholesale/

## What makes it different

The north-south seam. MISO grew in two parts: the original northern footprint, and MISO South (Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and East Texas), which joined in 2013. The two are tied together by a narrow set of transmission links, so power often cannot flow freely between north and south, and prices on each side can differ. The north has a lot of wind and coal; the south has more natural gas and nuclear.

Sources: https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/ ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/dashboard/electric_overview/balancing_authority/MISO

## A short history

- **2001-12-20:** The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approves MISO as the first regional transmission organization (RTO) in the United States (MISO, https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/industry-foundations/miso-history/).
- **2005-04-01:** MISO opens its day-ahead and real-time energy markets (FERC, https://ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-05/miso-06-30-05.pdf).
- **2013-12-19:** Utilities in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and East Texas join MISO as MISO South (FERC, https://ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-05/E-4_84.pdf).

Sources: https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/

## Glossary

- **Balancing authority:** the organization that keeps supply and demand equal in an area. EIA reports MISO as balancing authority MISO.
- **Regional transmission organization (RTO):** a grid operator that runs transmission and markets across several states.
- **Demand:** how much electricity customers are using, in megawatts (MW).
- **Megawatt (MW) and megawatt-hour (MWh):** a megawatt is a rate of power; a megawatt-hour is one megawatt for one hour, an amount of energy.
- **Net generation:** the power plants produce, minus what they use themselves.
- **Day-ahead market:** trades for each hour of tomorrow, agreed today.
- **Real-time market:** the price paid for power at the moment it is delivered.
- **Hub:** an average of many grid locations' prices, used as one reference price; this page uses the Indiana Hub.
- **Seam:** a boundary between parts of the grid where power cannot flow freely.
- **Carbon intensity:** the carbon dioxide released per megawatt-hour of electricity, in kilograms of CO2 per MWh.

Sources: https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/about ; https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/

questions.question: In June 2026, how much higher or lower was the load-weighted real-time price at ERCOT's hub average than at CAISO's SP15 hub, in USD per MWh?
questions.answer: In June 2026 (local month, complete at 720 real-time hours at both hubs), ERCOT's hub average was higher than CAISO's SP15 hub by 15.71 USD/MWh (cost_of_power_monthly, derived). ERCOT HB_HUBAVG load-weighted real-time price was 29.40 USD/MWh and CAISO TH_SP15_GEN-APND was 13.69 USD/MWh (cost_of_power_monthly). The difference is 15.7097 USD/MWh before rounding, from the compare tool. These are wholesale energy prices only, weighted by hourly demand.

questions.question: What was the load-weighted real-time price at PJM's Western hub in August 2026, in USD per MWh?
questions.answer: Not in the warehouse. It holds no PJM energy prices, so it has no real-time price at PJM's Western hub. The cost_of_power_monthly table, which carries the load-weighted real-time price, covers only CAISO, ERCOT, ISO-NE, MISO, NYISO and SPP. PJM is absent from it.
